source_text:
ὅταν δὲ λέγωμεν σῶμα ἄφθαρτον, οὐ
πέμπτην οὐσίαν λέγομεν, ὥς τινες περὶ τῶν ἄστρων ὑπενόησαν ἣν ἀεί φαμεν ἄφθαρτον εἶναι, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτον λέγομεν τὸ ἐκ φθαρτοῦ γεγονὸς ἄφθαρτον χάριτι θεοῦ. οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν ἤτοι κολαζόμενον ἢ τιμώμενον. 1 Kor 15,44-46 Ἐπειδὴ σπείρεται τὸ σῶμα ἐκ τῆς περιπλοκῆς τοῦ ἄρρενος πρὸς τὸ θῆλυ, εὐλόγως καὶ ἀτιμία καὶ ἀσθένεια περὶ αὐτὸ ἔσται, τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος, ἀνίσταται θεοῦ δυνάμει, ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ τιμὴν ἔχον πνευματικὸν σῶμα ἀποδειχθέν, ὄργανον ψυχῆς ὑπάρχον, λοιπὸν οὐ ψυχῆς ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου μετουσίᾳ ἀνασταθείσης καὶ οἱονεὶ εἰς πνεῦμα μεταβαλούσης. ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἡ τοῖς πάθεσιν ἐμμένουσα ψυχή, εἰκότως καὶ τὸ τῆς τοιαύτης ψυχῆς σῶμα ψυχικὸν καλεῖται. ἐὰν δὲ ὑπεραναβῇ τὴν παθητικὴν ἕξιν ἡ ψυχή, γίνεται πνευματική, καὶ λέγεται τὸ σῶμα τῆς τοιαύτης ψυχῆς τῆς συμπλεκομένης αὐτὸ πνευματικόν. Ἐπειδὴ προκόπτουσα ἡ ψυχὴ ἐπὶ τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀναβαίνει, πρῶτον εἶπεν εἶναι τὸ ψυχικὸν σῶμα, ἔπειτα τὸ πνευματικόν. νοητέον δὲ ὅτι τὸ τῶν ἐγειρομένων ἐκ νεκρῶν σῶμα ὁμοιοῦται τῷ τοῦ Χριστοῦ σώματι πνευματικῷ μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν γεγονότι. διὸ οὐ προσέχομεν τοῖς λέγουσιν ὅτι τοιοῦτον ἀνίσταται τὸ σῶμα οἷον εἶχεν ὁ Ἀδὰμ ψυχικόν· ἡ μὲν οὖν τοῦ πρώτου Ἀδὰμ ζωὴ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν παρεσκεύαζε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ζῆν, ἡ δὲ κατὰ Χριστὸν ζωὴ οὐκ εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν ἀλλ' εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν. ἡ δὲ πνευματικὴ ζωοποίησις συμφυής ἐστι τοῖς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγειρομένοις. πρῶτον δὲ καὶ ἔσχατον ἁρμοδίως εἶπεν, οὐ μὴν πρῶτον καὶ δεύτερον ἄνθρωπον, ἵνα μάθωμεν ὅτι γεγόνασί τινες μέσοι, τοῦ πρώτου καὶ ἐσχάτου ἀνθρώπου ἐν πολιτείᾳ. 11 1 Kor 15,51 Ἐπειδὴ περὶ ἀναστάσεως θεωρία βάθος ἔχειν νοήσεως, εἰκότως φησίν· ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος· μόνοι γὰρ οὗτοι ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον κατὰ ψυχὴν καὶ σῶμα μεταβάλλοντες ἀλλαγήσονται. οὐ γὰρ ἀκόλουθον λέγειν ἐν ἀλλάξει κατά τινα ἑτέραν φερομένην οὕτω γραφήν· οὐ πάντες μὲν κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα διὰ τὸ εὐθὺς ἐπιφερόμενον καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα. εἰ γὰρ πάντες ἀλλάττονται, περιττὸν λέγεσθαι καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα. 1 Kor 15,52-53 Ἐγερθήσονται οἱ νεκροὶ τοῦ σώματος αὐτῶν, ὃ πάλαι φθαρτὸν ἦν, ἀφθάρτου γενησομένου. τινὲς δὲ λέγουσιν ὧδε τὸ ἡ μεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς, οἵτινες, φησίν, ἄφθαρτοι ἐγειρόμεθα τὰ σώματα, ἀλλασσομενῶν τῶν ψυχῶν κατὰ κρείττονα καὶ θειοτέραν ποιότητα ἀλλοιουμενῶν. ἄλλος δέ φησι τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἶναι τοὺς νεκρούς, τοὺς ἀφθάρτους ἐγειρομένους ἐπὶ τῷ διαρκέσαι πρὸς τὰς αἰωνίους κολάσεις, ἀλλασσομένους δὲ ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν τοὺς κατ' ἀρετὴν βεβιωκότας· ἔστι μὲν οὖν θνητὸν καὶ φθαρτὸν οὐ μὴν ἔμπαλιν. διὸ τὸ φθαρτὸν ἀφθαρσίαν, τὸ δὲ θνητὸν ἀθανασίαν ἐνδύεται ἐν τῷ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν καιρῷ. 1 Kor 15,54-56 Ὥσπερ ἀρετῆς παρούσης οὐχ ὑπάρχει κακία, οὕτως ἀθανασίας παρούσης ὁ θάνατος ἀφανίζεται. διὸ τοῦ θνητοῦ τὴν ἀθανασίαν ἐνδυσαμένου ὁ θάνατος ἡττηθεὶς καταπίνεται, ὡς λέγεσθαι αὐτῷ· ποῦ σου τὸ νῖκος ἐν ᾧ νικῶν νεκροὺς ἐποίεις; ποῦ σου τὸ κέντρον ᾧ τιτρώσκων ἰσχυρὸς ἦς; κεντεῖ μὲν γὰρ κατὰ τοὺς λογισμοὺς ἐμβάλλων ἁμαρτίας τοῖς πληττομένοις ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, νικᾷ δὲ τοὺς πρακτικῶς ἁμαρτάνοντας. κεῖται δὲ ἡ χρῆσις ἐν Ὠσηὲ οὐκ αὐταῖς λέξεσιν· ἀντὶ γὰρ τοῦ ἡ δίκη 3 σου ὁ ἀπόστολος εἶπε νῖκος. 1 Kor 15,58 Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἐχθρὸς θάνατος κατελύθη, πιστῶς ἑστηκότες ἑδραῖοι διατελεῖτε, ἐργαζόμενοι συνεχῶς καὶ ἀδιασπάστως τὸ προσταχθὲν ὑμῖν 12 ἔργον ὑπὸ κυρίου, ἀδιστάκτως θαρροῦντες, ὡς ὁ ἐν κυρίῳ κάματος ὑμῶν οὐκ ἔστι μάταιος, αἰωνίου μισθοῦ ἀποκειμένου τοῖς πάντοτε τὸ ἔργον ποιοῦσιν.
thought_title: The risen body is incorruptible by grace, not a fifth substance; the spiritual body and the change of the righteous
orientation: Didymus is expounding 1 Corinthians 15:44-58, explaining what Paul means by the natural body and the spiritual body, and correcting alternative readings of the resurrection and the change.
pass_a_gloss: But when we say an incorruptible body, we do not say a fifth substance, as some have supposed about the stars, which we always say is incorruptible, but we say incorruptible that which has come to be from a corruptible thing incorruptible by the grace of God. Thus it is unchangeable and unalterable according to change, for such a thing came into being, but by enduring into long-lasting life either being punished or being honored. Since the body is sown from the intertwining of the male with the female, reasonably both dishonor and weakness will be about it, being a body of a soul, the previous quality having been corrupted in it, it is raised by the power of God, having incorruptibility and power and honor, having been shown to be a spiritual body, being an instrument of the soul, no longer simply of the soul, but of the soul raised by participation in the Holy Spirit and as it were changing into spirit. But since the soul that remains in the passions, reasonably also the body of such a soul is called natural. But if the soul goes beyond the passible state, it becomes spiritual, and the body of such a soul that is intertwined with it is called spiritual. Since the soul advancing goes up to the spiritual, he said first that the natural body is, then the spiritual. But it must be understood that the body of those raised from the dead is made like the spiritual body of Christ that came to be after the resurrection. Therefore we do not attend to those who say that the body is raised such as Adam had, natural. For the life of the first Adam prepared the man to live as a living soul, but the life according to Christ is not into a living soul but into a life-giving spirit. But the spiritual making alive is natural to those raised from the dead. But he said first and last fittingly, not first and second man, so that we may learn that some have been in the middle, in the conduct of the first and last man. Since the contemplation about the resurrection has depth of understanding, reasonably he says: behold I tell you a mystery: all of us who are going to die will sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining as the sun. For only these, changing for the better in soul and body, will be changed. For it is not consistent to say in a change according to some other reading that is carried thus: not all will sleep, but all will be changed, because of what is immediately brought in: and we will be changed. For if all are changed, it is superfluous to say also we will be changed. The dead will be raised, their body, which long ago was corruptible, being about to become incorruptible. But some say here the we will be changed instead of as being some others besides the dead, who, he says, are raised incorruptible in bodies, the souls being changed and altered according to a better and more divine quality. But another says that the sinners are the dead, raised incorruptible for enduring to the eternal punishments, but those who have lived according to virtue are changed from glory to glory. So there is mortal and corruptible, but not the reverse. Therefore the corruptible puts on incorruptibility, and the mortal puts on immortality at the time of the resurrection of the dead. Just as when virtue is present vice does not exist, so when immortality is present death is destroyed. Therefore when the mortal has put on immortality, death, being defeated, is swallowed up, so that it is said to it: where is your victory in which you conquered and made dead? Where is your sting with which you wounded and were strong? For it stings according to the thoughts, casting sins into those struck by it, and it conquers those who sin in action. But the usage lies in Hosea not in the same words: for instead of your justice the apostle said victory. Since the enemy death has been destroyed, standing faithfully remain steadfast, working continually and without interruption the work commanded to you by the Lord, taking courage without doubting, since your labor in the Lord is not vain, an eternal reward being laid up for those who always do the work.

choices.why: Didymus is refuting the idea that the incorruptible risen body is a distinct fifth element, as some supposed about the stars; 'substance' preserves the philosophical term οὐσία.
The glossary requires 'natural body' for the body animated by the soul and subject to corruption.
The glossary requires 'spiritual body' for the risen body transformed by the Holy Spirit.
The glossary requires 'we will be changed' for the change of the righteous at the resurrection.
The glossary requires 'victory' for νῖκος, and Didymus notes Paul used it instead of 'justice' from Hosea.
The glossary requires 'sting' for κέντρον, the sting of death identified with sin.

pass_b_english: But when we speak of an incorruptible body, we are not speaking of a fifth substance, as some have supposed about the stars, which we say is always incorruptible. Rather, we call incorruptible what has become incorruptible from a corruptible state by the grace of God. In the same way, it is unchangeable and unalterable not in the sense of undergoing change—for it became incorruptible through change—but in the sense of enduring into long-lasting life, whether being punished or being honored. Since the body is sown from the intertwining of male with female, it is reasonable that dishonor and weakness will also attend it, since it is a natural body, being a body of a soul, the prior quality of which was corrupted in it. It is raised by the power of God, possessing incorruptibility and power and honor, shown to be a spiritual body, an instrument of the soul—no longer simply of the soul, but of the soul that has been raised by participation in the Holy Spirit and has, as it were, been changed into spirit. And since the soul that remains in the passions is such, the body of such a soul is also rightly called a natural body. But if the soul rises above the passionate condition, it becomes spiritual, and the body of such a soul, which is intertwined with it, is called a spiritual body. Since the soul, as it advances, ascends to the spiritual, Paul first said that the natural body exists, then the spiritual. And it must be understood that the body of those raised from the dead is made like the spiritual body of Christ, which came into being after the resurrection. Therefore we do not pay attention to those who say that the body is raised such as Adam had, a natural body. For the life of the first Adam prepared the human being to live as a living soul, but the life according to Christ is not into a living soul but into a life-giving spirit. And this spiritual making alive is proper to those raised from the dead. Paul fittingly said first and last man, not first and second man, so that we might learn that there have been some in between, in the conduct of the first and last man. Since the contemplation of the resurrection has depth of understanding, Paul reasonably says: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun." For only these, changing for the better in soul and body, will be changed. For it is not consistent to say, according to another reading that is circulated, "we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed," because of what is immediately added: "and we will be changed." For if all are changed, it is superfluous to say "and we will be changed." The dead will be raised with their body, which was formerly corruptible but will become incorruptible. But some say that here "we will be changed" means that we are some others besides the dead, who, they say, are raised with incorruptible bodies, while their souls are changed and altered for a better and more divine quality. Another says that the sinners are the dead, who are raised incorruptible so as to endure eternal punishments, while those who have lived according to virtue are changed from glory to glory. Now what is mortal is also corruptible, but not the reverse. Therefore the corruptible puts on incorruptibility, and the mortal puts on immortality, at the time of the resurrection of the dead. Just as when virtue is present, vice does not exist, so when immortality is present, death is destroyed. Therefore, when the mortal has put on immortality, death is defeated and swallowed up, so that it is said to it: "Where is your victory, by which you conquered and made people dead? Where is your sting, by which you wounded and were strong?" For it stings by casting sins into the thoughts of those struck by it, and it conquers those who sin in deed. The usage derives from Hosea, not in the same words: for instead of "your justice" the apostle said "victory" (Hosea 13:14 LXX, adapted by Paul). Since the enemy death has been destroyed, stand firm and remain steadfast in faith, working continually and without interruption the work commanded you by the Lord, taking courage without doubt, since your labor in the Lord is not in vain, an eternal reward being laid up for those who always do the work.
notes: The source contains a lacuna marked by ** after κατὰ μεταβολήν; the gloss renders what is present and notes the break in the clause.

problems.quote: the previous quality in it having been corrupted
problems.source_quote: τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος
problems.why: Source says the body is a natural body, the soul's prior quality having been corrupted in it. English omits 'soul' and garbles the syntax.
problems.fix: being a natural body, the soul's prior quality having been corrupted in it
problems.ruling: Greek says ‘body of a corruptible soul’; English omits ‘soul’ and changes clause meaning.

problems.quote: And since the soul that remains in the passions is rightly called natural
problems.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἡ τοῖς πάθεσιν ἐμμένουσα ψυχή, εἰκότως καὶ τὸ τῆς τοιαύτης ψυχῆς σῶμα ψυχικὸν καλεῖται
problems.why: Source says the soul remaining in passions is 'psychic/natural'; English says the soul is 'called natural,' dropping the body clause's causal link.
problems.fix: And since the soul that remains in the passions is such, the body of such a soul is also rightly called a natural body
problems.ruling: Greek links soul remaining in passions to body being called psychic; English drops body clause and mis‑renders ‘psychic’ as ‘natural’.

problems.quote: And this spiritual making alive is natural to those raised from the dead.
problems.source_quote: ἡ δὲ πνευματικὴ ζωοποίησις συμφυής ἐστι τοῖς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγειρομένοις
problems.why: συμφυής means 'congenital, innate, akin,' not 'natural to.' The rendering confuses the claim.
problems.fix: And this spiritual making-alive is congenital to those raised from the dead.

we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed

problems.why: 'Congenital' means present from birth; resurrection life is not congenital
problems.fix: proper to or inherent in those raised

problems.why: 'Lies in' is unclear; means 'the usage derives from' or 'is found in'

Cited as source for 'victory' but Paul quotes 'Death, where is your victory?' from Hosea; however LXX Hosea 13:14 has 'your justice' not 'victory', which Didymus notes—yet he still cites Hosea as 'usage' when Paul modified it
problems.fix: Note: Paul adapts LXX Hosea, changing 'justice' to 'victory'

problems.quote: it is unchangeable and unalterable not in the sense of undergoing change—for such a thing came into being through change—but in the sense of enduring into long-lasting life
problems.why: Double negative and 'such a thing' make the logic hard to follow; 'came into being through change' is unclear.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'not meaning it cannot change—for it became incorruptible through change—but that it endures permanently…'

problems.quote: Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.
problems.why: This merges 1 Cor 15:51 with Didymus's interpretation without distinction; 'die and sleep' is not the standard text.
problems.fix: Separate the biblical quote from the interpretation, or mark 'we will all die and sleep' as Didymus's reading.

problems.quote: Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.
problems.why: 1 Cor 15:51 in standard texts reads 'We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed'; this quote reverses the meaning.
problems.fix: Note that Didymus argues for this reading against the standard one, or correct the quote.

problems.quote: For if all are changed, it is superfluous to say "and we will be changed."
problems.why: The logic is circular and hard to follow: if 'we will all be changed' is the reading, repeating 'we will be changed' is not necessarily superfluous.
problems.fix: Clarify the argument: Didymus says the phrase 'and we will be changed' is redundant if 'all' are already said to be changed.

problems.quote: Where is your victory, by which you conquered and made people dead? Where is your sting, by which you wounded and were strong?
problems.why: This reads as an expanded paraphrase of 1 Cor 15:55 but the added clauses ('made people dead,' 'were strong') are awkward.
problems.fix: Mark as Didymus's expanded paraphrase, or streamline: 'Where is your victory? Where is your sting?'

problems.quote: for instead of "your justice" the apostle said "victory" (Hosea 13:14)
problems.why: Hosea 13:14 in the LXX reads 'Where is your penalty/punishment (dikē)?' not 'your justice (dikaiosynē)'; the comparison is unclear.
problems.fix: Clarify the LXX reading of Hosea 13:14 and what word Paul changed.

edits.old: Where is your victory, by which you conquered and made people dead? Where is your sting, by which you wounded and were strong?
edits.new: Where is your victory, by which you conquered and made people dead? Where is your sting, by which you wounded and were strong?

fixed: The English 'it is unchangeable and unalterable not in the sense of undergoing change—for such a thing came into being through change—but in the sense of enduring into long-lasting life' is unclear because 'such a thing' is vague. The source says 'οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν' — 'Thus it is unchangeable and unalterable according to change, for such a thing came into being, but by enduring into long-lasting life.' The English misreads the logic: the body is unchangeable not by nature but by enduring. I changed 'such a thing came into being through change' to 'it became incorruptible through change' to clarify the referent.

The English 'congenital to those raised from the dead' is a mistranslation of 'συμφυής ἐστι τοῖς ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγειρομένοις'. 'Συμφυής' means 'grown together with, innate, natural to' but not 'congenital' in the sense of present from birth. The resurrection life is not present from birth. I changed to 'proper to'.

The English 'The usage lies in Hosea' is unclear. The source says 'κεῖται δὲ ἡ χρῆσις ἐν Ὠσηὲ' — 'the usage is found in Hosea'. 'Lies in' is ambiguous; 'derives from' better conveys that Paul's use of 'victory' comes from Hosea.

The English 'for instead of "your justice" the apostle said "victory" (Hosea 13:14)' is correct but the citation needs clarification. The source says 'ἀντὶ γὰρ τοῦ ἡ δίκη σου ὁ ἀπόστολος εἶπε νῖκος' — 'for instead of "your justice" the apostle said "victory"'. The LXX of Hosea 13:14 has 'ἡ δίκη σου' which means 'your justice' or 'your penalty'. Didymus notes Paul changed it. I added 'LXX, adapted by Paul' to clarify.

The English 'Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.' is a correct rendering of the source 'ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος'. Didymus is quoting his own reading of 1 Cor 15:51, not the standard text. The English already presents this as Didymus's quotation. No edit needed.

The English 'For if all are changed, it is superfluous to say "and we will be changed."' is a correct rendering of the source 'εἰ γὰρ πάντες ἀλλάττονται, περιττὸν λέγεσθαι καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα'. The logic is Didymus's own argument against the alternative reading. No edit needed.

The English 'Where is your victory, by which you conquered and made people dead? Where is your sting, by which you wounded and were strong?' is a correct rendering of the source 'ποῦ σου τὸ νῖκος ἐν ᾧ νικῶν νεκροὺς ἐποίεις; ποῦ σου τὸ κέντρον ᾧ τιτρώσκων ἰσχυρὸς ἦς;'. Didymus is expanding the biblical quotation with his own explanatory clauses. No edit needed.

dismissed.quote: it is reasonable that dishonor and weakness will also attend it, since it is a natural body
dismissed.why: The Greek lists honor (εὐλόγως) along with dishonor and weakness, but the English omits it.
dismissed.note: εὐλόγως is the adverb 'reasonably' (already rendered 'it is reasonable'), not the word 'honor', so nothing is omitted.
